name: Adult Autism Spectrum Quotient (AQ)
description: A 50-item self-administered instrument for measuring the degree to which an adult with normal intelligence has the traits associated with the autistic spectrum. The 50 questions are made up of 10 questions assessing five different areas: - social skill (items 1, 11, 13, 15, 22, 36, 44, 45, 47, 48); - attention switching (items 2, 4, 10, 16, 25, 32, 34, 37, 43, 46); - attention to detail (items 5, 6, 9, 12, 19, 23, 28, 29, 30, 49); - communication (items 7, 17, 18, 26, 27, 31, 33, 35, 38, 39); -
citation: Cohen S, Wheelwright S, Skinner R, Martin J, Clubley E (2001). The autism-spectrum quotient (AQ): evidence from Asperger syndrome/high-functioning autism, males and females, scientists and mathematicians. *J Autism Dev Disord.* 31(1): 5-17. Erratum in: *J Autism Dev Disord.* 2001 Dec;31(6):603. https://doi.org/10.1023/a:1005653411471 https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11439754/

name: Big Five Inventory-2
description: A 44-item measure of the Big Five personality traits (Extraversion, Agreeableness, Conscientiousness, Neuroticism, Openness) using short trait-descriptive phrases. Items use a 5-point scale (1=disagree strongly to 5=agree strongly). Several items are reverse-scored. Widely used in personality research across cultures. Originally developed in English; Swahili translation from Garrashi et al. (2023).
citation: John, O. P., Donahue, E. M., & Kentle, R. L. (1991). The Big Five Inventory—Versions 4a and 54. University of California, Berkeley, Institute of Personality and Social Research.
license: Non-commercial research use; freely available from Berkeley Personality Lab

name: Big Five Inventory-Short
description: 15-item short measure of the Big Five personality traits (3 items per trait). Scored as mean per dimension on a 1-7 scale.
citation: Lang, F. R., John, D., Ludtke, O., Schupp, J., & Wagner, G. G. (2011). Short assessment of the Big Five: Robust across survey methods except telephone interviewing. Behavior Research Methods, 43(2), 548-567. https://doi.org/10.3758/s13428-011-0066-z

name: Flourishing Scale
description: 8-item summary measure of psychological well-being covering social relationships, meaning, purpose, and self-esteem.
citation: Diener, E., Wirtz, D., Tov, W., Kim-Prieto, C., Choi, D., Oishi, S., & Biswas-Diener, R. (2010). New well-being measures: Short scales to assess flourishing and positive and negative feelings. Social Indicators Research, 97(2), 143–156. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11205-009-9493-y

name: General Self-Efficacy Scale
description: 10-item unidimensional self-report measure of general self-efficacy — the belief in one's overall competence to cope with challenging demands and difficult situations. Uses a 4-point Likert scale (1=Not at all true to 4=Exactly true). Scored as the sum of all 10 items (range 10–40); higher scores indicate greater self-efficacy. No reverse-coded items. Validated in over 30 countries with consistent unidimensional structure and high internal consistency. Available in 32 languages from the author's website.
citation: Schwarzer, R., & Jerusalem, M. (1995). Generalized Self-Efficacy scale. In J. Weinman, S. Wright, & M. Johnston (Eds.), Measures in health psychology: A user's portfolio. Causal and control beliefs (pp. 35–37). Windsor, UK: NFER-NELSON.
license: Free for research and professional use with attribution; not open-licensed

name: Multidimensional Scale of Perceived Social Support
description: 12-item self-report measure of perceived social support from three sources: Significant Other (items 1,2,5,10), Family (items 3,4,8,11), and Friends (items 6,7,9,12). Uses a 7-point Likert scale (1=Very Strongly Disagree to 7=Very Strongly Agree). Scoring is the mean per subscale and mean of all 12 items for the total scale. Widely validated across cultures and languages.
citation: Zimet, G. D., Dahlem, N. W., Zimet, S. G., & Farley, G. K. (1988). The Multidimensional Scale of Perceived Social Support. Journal of Personality Assessment, 52(1), 30–41.
license: Free for research and professional use with attribution; not open-licensed

name: Personality Inventory for DSM-5 Brief Form
description: 25-item brief self-report measure of the DSM-5 maladaptive personality trait model, covering five broad domains: Negative Affect, Detachment, Antagonism, Disinhibition, and Psychoticism. Each domain is assessed with 5 items scored 0–3.
citation: Krueger, R. F., Derringer, J., Markon, K. E., Watson, D., & Skodol, A. E. (2012). Initial construction of a maladaptive personality trait model and inventory for DSM-5. Psychological Medicine, 42(9), 1879–1890. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0033291711002674

name: Quadrangular Love Scale
description: 40-item self-report measure of love across four dimensions: Compassion (items 1–10), Affection (items 11–20), Closeness (items 21–30), and Commitment (items 31–40). Each subscale contains 10 items rated on a 7-point Likert scale. Compassion and Affection reflect feelings toward the partner; Closeness and Commitment reflect feelings about the relationship. Validated in US and UK samples with high internal consistency (α = .86–.93 per subscale). Items are presented in random order; researcher-only facet labels are not shown to participants.
citation: Karandashev, V., & Evans, N. D. (2019). Quadrangular love theory and scale: Validation and psychometric investigation. Journal of Methods and Measurement in the Social Sciences, 10(1), 1–35. https://doi.org/10.2458/v10i1.23520

name: Scale of Positive and Negative Experience
description: 12-item scale measuring positive (SPANE-P) and negative (SPANE-N) affect over the past four weeks, yielding an affect balance score (SPANE-B).
citation: Diener, E., Wirtz, D., Tov, W., Kim-Prieto, C., Choi, D., Oishi, S., & Biswas-Diener, R. (2010). New well-being measures: Short scales to assess flourishing and positive and negative feelings. Social Indicators Research, 97(2), 143–156. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11205-009-9493-y

name: WHO-5 Well-Being Index
description: 5-item measure of subjective well-being over the past 2 weeks. Raw score 0-25; percentage score (0-100) = raw score x 4. Scores of 50 or below suggest low mood warranting further assessment.
citation: Topp, C. W., Ostergaard, S. D., Sondergaard, S., & Bech, P. (2015). The WHO-5 Well-Being Index: A systematic review of the literature. Psychotherapy and Psychosomatics, 84(3), 167-176. https://doi.org/10.1159/000376585
